what_its_for: Nitazoxanide is an antiparasitic and antiviral medicine used to treat diarrhea caused by tiny parasites called Cryptosporidium parvum and Giardia lamblia (also called Giardia intestinalis). These parasites can get into your body through contaminated food or water and cause stomach cramps, nausea, and watery diarrhea.
how_to_take: Take nitazoxanide with food — this helps your body absorb the medicine better and reduces stomach upset. If you are taking the tablet form, swallow it whole with a full glass of water. If you are using the oral suspension (liquid), shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring spoon or oral syringe provided. Do not use a regular kitchen spoon, as it may not give you the right amount.
dosing: Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions. The usual dosing is: Adults and children 12 years and older: one 500 mg tablet (or 25 mL of oral suspension) twice a day for 3 days. Children 4 to 11 years: 10 mL of oral suspension twice a day for 3 days. Children 1 to 3 years: 5 mL of oral suspension twice a day for 3 days. Your doctor may adjust the dose based on your age, weight, and health condition. Always complete the full 3-day course even if you start to feel better.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them in a dry place away from light and moisture. Store the reconstituted (mixed) oral suspension at room temperature and use it within 7 days — throw away any leftover liquid after 7 days. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid sharing your medicine with others, even if they have similar symptoms. Avoid drinking untreated or potentially contaminated water, as this could cause reinfection. Practice good hand hygiene — wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the bathroom and before eating to prevent spreading the infection. There are no specific foods or drinks you must avoid, but eating bland, easy-to-digest foods may help soothe your stomach while you have diarrhea.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing; severe stomach pain or cramping that gets worse; bloody or black stools; high fever (above 102°F or 39°C); signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, little or no urination, dizziness, or feeling very weak; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); or if your diarrhea does not improve after finishing all 3 days of treatment.
when_it_works: Most people start to feel better within 1 to 3 days of starting treatment. The full 3-day course is important to completely clear the infection. If your symptoms do not improve after finishing all doses, let your doctor know, as you may need further testing or a different treatment.
special_populations: Children under 1 year of age: Safety and effectiveness have not been established — do not use without specific guidance from a doctor. Pregnant women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Use nitazoxanide during pregnancy only if your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk. Breastfeeding mothers: It is not fully known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Patients with liver or kidney disease: Use with caution. Your doctor may need to monitor you more closely or adjust your dose. Elderly patients: No specific dose adjustment is usually needed, but your doctor will consider your overall health.
